notes: Engine behaviour, found with synthetic probe tasks run through teacher_check.py --bank <my scratch file> (the manifest was not read): description constants ON, tie_break ON, named_pairs OFF, and the match list behaves as if keep_best were OFF (first 40 matches in enumeration order). Consequences for every pack: a fully named one-step coincidence (score 1.7) always beats a fully named two-step program (1.4), and a two-step program is lost when the expected value is reproduced many times at level 1 (MbppX/190). Enabling named_pairs or 4-ary operators would open slope (835), rectangle lattice points (190) and interval endpoints (660); keep_best would let the square reading of 190 through. A temporary probe operator (probe_max_r4n) was used once to test the tie-break and removed. Risky operators: chinese_zodiac_r4n uses Rabbit and Goat where the bank reference writes 'Hare' and lowercase 'sheep', so tests copied from such references differ for those two years; most_frequent_divisor_r4n ships the closed form `b if a == b else 2` (proved and brute-force checked for a < b; a == b answers the number itself by the tasks' convention); equilateral_triangles_in_r4n returns -1 when k > n (the tasks' convention) and counts inverted triangles correctly where the bank reference over-counts for k <= n < 2k - 1 (n = k = 3: reference 2, operator 1); filled_grid_r4n is generic and opens on 'two-dimensional|2d array|3d array|filled with|each element as' but only builds from two ints in 1..30 and a scalar, so it cannot fire on list tasks. Cross-pack dependency: the keyword extension of seq_repeat_whole/2 needs r3_sequences loaded first and is skipped (not raised) otherwise. Helper names carry the _r4n suffix to avoid collisions with other packs' helpers in one answer. All closed forms were checked against brute force in outputs/rule_round4/scratch_r4_numbers/verify_formulas.py; fn and template equality, bool gating, no mutation, determinism and speed were checked with a mock-lib linter (scratch packcheck.py). Gate keywords beyond the bank wording are plain paraphrases (e.g. 'square numbers&between', 'cubes of side'), not taken from known tasks; the name 'Bytelandian' is the general name of the coin-splitting problem.
